title: Crypto spent $233 million on Congress. North Korea spent 20 minutes on Binance.
dek: The industry became America's biggest corporate political spender, its rulebook died in the Senate over an ethics clause, and the largest crypto theft on record was covered by a pinky promise. A look at who's minding the vault.
body:
## Twenty minutes on a Thursday

Let's start with a unit of time. Twenty minutes. That is roughly how long it takes to microwave a frozen lasagna properly, to sit through the pre-roll ads on a streaming service you already pay for, or, as of last Thursday, to steal more than six billion dollars from the biggest crypto exchange on Earth.

On October 29, an attacker moved about $6.36 billion out of Binance wallets across ten blockchains, "most of it in about 20 minutes," according to the blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs, which attributed the attack "with high confidence" to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking unit [2]. TechCrunch reported that TRM called it the "largest hack in history," and that Elliptic, another tracing firm, also pinned it on North Korea and found some of the stolen money landing in the same wallet used in a $351 million attack on the exchange Bitget earlier this year [1]. The same unit was blamed by the FBI for the 2025 hack of Bybit, which cost that exchange $1.5 billion [2]. So this is not a new villain. This is a returning villain who came back for the sequel with a bigger budget.

And researchers say the point of these heists is to fund a sanctioned weapons program [1]. Which means somewhere in Pyongyang there is an accounting department that has had a better quarter than most of the S&P 500.

## How you rob a vault that isn't a vault

Binance's first explanation was the most relatable thing a multinational has said all year: an engineer's laptop got "compromised," which "allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions" [1]. Everyone who has ever clicked a suspicious attachment felt seen. Binance later said it had found additional "points of breach" and no evidence of a leaked private key [2].

Chief executive Richard Teng then explained that the attackers used EIP-7702, an Ethereum feature, to get execution approval over a "hot wallet," the online wallet that pays out withdrawals, and that "that delegation did not pass through our normal approval controls" [3]. A cybersecurity founder quoted by the Associated Press, NyxLab's Kok Tin Gan, put it more bluntly: "This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet" [2]. That's not a security breach. That's handing a stranger a key to the building and writing "good forever" on it in Sharpie.

About $3 billion was frozen by industry partners as the money moved [1]. Binance suspended deposits and withdrawals and said "user funds are safe," without immediately offering proof; it did not answer TechCrunch's questions about the breach, including whether anyone outside the company had audited its security beforehand [1]. Teng later said the company had set aside more than $6.34 billion of its own money and would cover every dollar: "Your assets are safe," he said, adding, "We never use any customer funds, so they are not impacted" [3]. Founder Changpeng Zhao, who goes by CZ, summarized the mood on social media: "It hurts, but we survive" [3].

Here's the thing worth sitting with. For millions of customers, the safety net for a $6 billion theft turned out to be one company deciding, voluntarily, in a video address, to be nice about it [3]. Binance says it can afford that because it keeps much of its operating earnings in crypto [3]. Great. And if it couldn't? There's no federal rule here that says what happens next. Which brings us to Washington, where a lot of people have been very well paid to talk about that rule and not pass it.

## A brief and expensive history of Binance

To be fair to Binance, this is not the first time it has had a rough day with the United States. On November 21, 2023, the company pleaded guilty to conspiring to violate the Bank Secrecy Act, failing to register as a money transmitting business and violating sanctions law, and agreed to pay $4.3 billion and accept an independent monitor [6]. The Justice Department said Binance "prioritized growth, market share, and profits over compliance with U.S. law" [6]. Zhao pleaded guilty the same day to causing Binance to fail to maintain an effective anti-money-laundering program [6]. In court he said, "I failed here" [7].

Then, in October 2025, President Trump pardoned him [7]. The White House's press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, said the Biden administration had prosecuted Zhao out of a "desire to punish the cryptocurrency industry," and that there were "no allegations of fraud or identifiable victims" [7]. PBS noted the context: the Trump family's crypto venture, World Liberty Financial, had announced that a UAE-based fund would use $2 billion of its USD1 stablecoin to buy a stake in Binance, and Trump's disclosure showed he had earned more than $57 million from the venture the previous year [7].

None of that caused last week's hack; a laptop and a signature did [1][3]. But it does tell you how Washington has decided to treat the company that, as of Thursday, holds the record for the largest theft in crypto history [2]. The government's last word on Binance's compliance was a guilty plea. Its latest word on its founder was a pardon. And its word on what an exchange owes its customers when the vault empties in twenty minutes is: still drafting.

## The shopping cart

Now, you'd think an industry with that track record would keep its head down. Instead, it has become the single biggest corporate spender in American elections.

According to a Public Citizen analysis of spending through October 23, corporations have put a record $737.3 million into the 2026 midterms, roughly four times what they spent in 2022, and crypto companies account for $233 million of it [8]. The single largest corporate contributor is the venture firm Andreessen Horowitz at $76.2 million, followed in the crypto column by Ripple Labs at $49.6 million and Coinbase at $37.2 million [8]. The crypto super PAC Fairshake received $106.9 million from corporations [8]. For comparison, fossil fuel companies, an industry that has historically never been shy about Congress, spent $51.4 million [8]. Big Oil has been out-lobbied by a sector whose main product is, in some cases, a dog picture.

A CNBC report, as summarized by Newsmax, said the industry is putting more than $200 million into congressional races, after crypto-backed super PACs spent $250 million in 2024 [9]. Fairshake's House slate this time is 33 candidates, 19 Republicans and 14 Democrats, with at least $1 million each for six incumbents: Republicans Bryan Steil, French Hill and Bill Huizenga, all of whom sit on committees covering financial services and digital assets, and Democrats Janelle Bynum, Derek Tran and Steven Horsford [9]. That's the beauty of it. It's not partisan. It's a bipartisan commitment to whoever might write the rules.

Coinbase's vice chairman, Ryan VanGrack, told CNBC that "the ultimate goal is to make sure that we bring our 20th century financial system into the 21st century" [9]. Which is a lovely line, and also exactly what you'd say if your goal were a rulebook you helped write.

## The bill they paid for, and how it died

So what did $233 million buy? The bill at the center of all this is the CLARITY Act, which would set up the country's first regulatory framework for digital asset markets [4]. The House passed it 294 to 134 in July 2025 [10]. Then it went to the Senate, where bills go to be admired.

On September 15, 2026, the Senate failed to advance it, 49 to 50, short of the 60 votes needed [10]. Democrats voted against it as a bloc, joined by Republicans Susan Collins, Josh Hawley and Jerry Moran; Thom Tillis voted yes, switched to no and filed a motion to reconsider, so the thing can be dragged back for a lame-duck vote [10]. FinTech Weekly's tracker lists the reasons: ethics provisions meant to stop senior officials from keeping business ties to crypto companies, a fight between crypto platforms and banks over paying interest-like yield on stablecoins, money-laundering concerns from Democrats such as Andy Kim, and the calendar [10]. Cointelegraph put it more simply: it stalled over proposed rules that would restrict government officials and their families from issuing or profiting from digital assets while in office [4].

Read that again. The single biggest corporate political spending spree in modern American history ran aground, in part, on the question of whether the people writing crypto rules should be allowed to own crypto businesses [4][10]. That's not a policy disagreement. That's a conflict-of-interest clause walking into a room and everybody suddenly remembering an appointment.

Both parties get to own a piece of this. Democrats wanted an ethics rule aimed squarely at a president whose family sells a stablecoin [4][7]. Some Republicans sided with banks, which feared that letting crypto pay yield would pull deposits away from them; Punchbowl News counted seven of them [10]. And the industry, which spent more than every other corporate sector, could not buy its way past either the banks or the conflict-of-interest problem [8][10]. It turns out there's one lobby in Washington that's older and more patient than crypto, and it's the one with marble lobbies.

## Everyone's hot take is about the other guy

After the hack, Washington did what it does best: issued statements. Sen. Cynthia Lummis, a Wyoming Republican, posted that "hackers stole more than $6 billion from Binance in less than 4 hours, the biggest heist in history," and argued the stalled bill would have let firms freeze suspicious transactions faster when law enforcement asks [4]. "Every minute lost is money gone for good," she wrote [5]. Amanda Fischer of the advocacy group Better Markets disputed that, arguing voluntary freezes were already possible and the bill wouldn't have changed that [5].

Rep. Maxine Waters, a California Democrat, called the hack "a wake-up call to anyone who thinks the cryptocurrency industry can operate without strong accountability," and blamed Trump and congressional Republicans for a deregulatory agenda, citing the pardon and the World Liberty deal [4]. The president, asked about it at a news conference, said: "We don't know. We're looking at that, the hack with Binance" [4].

And the one regulator who actually has a job here, Commodity Futures Trading Commission Chair Michael Selig, said the hack "proves our exact point in proposing regulations for crypto markets," while calling the real problem "unregulated offshore exchanges" [4]. His proposal is to offer exchanges like Binance a voluntary "federal option to come and register with the CFTC," because, as Bitcoin.com noted, Washington can't make every exchange register without more authority from Congress [5]. Public comments are open until December 14 [5]. Selig, by the way, is currently the commission's only member [10]. One commissioner, one voluntary sign-up sheet, one $6 billion hole. It's like answering a bank robbery by putting a suggestion box in the lobby.

## Who pays

Here's the part that gets lost when the people in the hearing rooms are arguing about whose fault it is. About half of the stolen money was frozen as it moved; the rest went where North Korea's money goes [1]. Customers had their money locked while the exchange rebuilt its systems [3]. The ones who got lucky got lucky because a single company with a guilty plea on its record decided to absorb the loss and could afford to [3][6]. The policy, in other words, is hope.

Meanwhile, the money that might have built a real rulebook went into campaign ads. Coinbase's own pitch for the spending leaned on affordability: cheaper transfers, easier investing, faster transactions [9]. You know what would make crypto more affordable? Not having it stolen by a government with a missile program.

## What would actually fix it

None of this is complicated, which is the most frustrating thing about it.

First, pass the ethics rule. The bill died partly because senators couldn't agree that officials and their families shouldn't profit from the industry they're regulating [4][10]. That should be the easiest vote in the building. If the industry really wants rules, it can spend some of its $233 million telling its friends to vote for that one [8].

Second, write actual safety requirements into whatever passes: custody standards for hot wallets, approval controls that can't be bypassed by one signature, independent security audits and a clear answer on who covers customers when it all goes wrong [2][3]. Right now, a voluntary registration offer is the government's best tool, because Congress hasn't given regulators more [5].

Third, give the regulators people. A commission with one member is not a commission. It's a guy [10].

And fourth, maybe treat a guilty plea for failing to stop money laundering as something other than a resume item [6][7].

The CLARITY Act has been waiting for the Senate since July 2025 [10]. North Korea needed about twenty minutes [2]. Tomorrow, voters decide who gets the next shot at writing the rules [9]. Whoever wins, here's a modest benchmark: try to be faster than the guys who robbed the place. You have a head start. You've had about fifteen months.

pt.title: O cripto gastou US$ 233 milhões no Congresso. A Coreia do Norte gastou 20 minutos na Binance.
pt.dek: O setor virou o maior gastador corporativo da política americana, sua lei morreu no Senado por causa de uma cláusula de ética, e o maior roubo de cripto da história foi coberto com uma promessa de dedinho. Quem está cuidando do cofre?

de.title: Krypto gab 233 Millionen Dollar für den Kongress aus. Nordkorea brauchte 20 Minuten für Binance.
de.dek: Die Branche ist Amerikas größter Firmenspender in der Politik, ihr Gesetz scheiterte im Senat an einer Ethikklausel, und der größte Kryptodiebstahl aller Zeiten wurde mit einem Ehrenwort abgedeckt. Wer passt eigentlich auf den Tresor auf?
